messages.subject: Effect of unused parameters?
parts:
Hey everyone,

In some of my models, I am using a ragged array of sorts.
E.g., I may use:

vector[K] mu[K];
in which I may only actually *use* mu[1,1], mu[2,1:2], mu[3,1:3], and so on.
I place priors only on the mu values I use, and thus not on, e.g., mu[1,2:K].
I then only ever use those mus (and thus, not mu[1,2:K], mu[2:3:K]) in the likelihood where appropriate.

In the output of course, HMC allows the particles to float off indefinitely, so the mean may be huge (and the sd infinite).
I've thought this is 'fine' and just a quirky side effect of having unconstrained and unused parameters.

However, are there implications for convergence and inference for the used variables?

Jim

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Effect of unused parameters?
parts:
Yes, extra parameters with no priors can severely mess up adaptation.
But they’re also just ill-defined and _shouldn’t_ fit.  Because HMC samples 
so efficiently it immediately identifies these “flat” parameters by running off 
to infinity, while other samplers slowly diffuse which can make it difficult to 
identify the problem.

So if you have to have ragged parameters then give them reasonable priors.
You’ll make adaptation easier if the priors are centered around zero and have
the same scale as your posterior standard deviations.  normal(0, scale) would
work well.

The performance of HMC scales really well with additional parameters, so
with proper priors you shouldn’t affect performance too much (the biggest
hit will probably be the I/O overhead for having to save the extra parameters)
but in the end having ancillary parameters is just another place where you
could mess something up so it’s always best to remove them if you can.

parts:
You could do something like this:

data {
 int<lower=0,upper=1> flag; // switch (0 or 1)
 int K; // size of parameter vector if flag is 1
}
parameters {
 real x[flag * K];
}
model {
 if (flag == 1) {
   // do something with x
 }
}


Would that work in your situation?

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Effect of unused parameters?
parts:
You mean something like this:

model {
theta ~ normal(if_else(fit_mean, mu, 0),
if_else(fit_sigma, sigma, 1));

where fit_mean and fit_sigma are int<lower=0, upper=1>
flags as Jonah indicated.

As long as you give mu and sigma proper priors it should work,
but it's going to make the models very hard to read. The
alternative is a lot of cut-and-paste, which is also not ideal.

I just modified my most needed (and one of the most problematic) models to include priors for unused parameters, and it *worked*.

Bob, if you recall my previous thread about the slow or halted warm-up, you may recall that my trace plots were extremely flat, with several thousand divergent transitions.

Now I have 0 divergent transitions and all chains are converging.

I'm not sure this is stated in the manual anywhere, but given that it turned this model from a trainwreck to a perfectly functioning model implies that perhaps the manual, if it doesn't already, should mention the effects of unrestricted parameters.

That is - parameters that are unrestricted by the data or by priors cause terrible sampling due to, I assume, terrible adaptation among other possible geometric problems.

I see. I will read the chapter, however from your answer I'm understanding that unbounded parameters (although with proper priors) are somehow harmful for the model.

Is this correct?

To answer your question

=================================================

I have 7 parameters of which only one is part of the naive model (LDA with phi known), and thus necessary.

  //-------------------------------//
  //   topic probability           //
  //-------------------------------//

  simplex[K] theta[M];   // topic distribution for doc m

  //-------------------------------//
  //   linear regression           //
  //-------------------------------//

  vector<lower=1-0.1, upper=maxPoly+1+0.1>[M] sigma; //activation/disease state
  vector<lower=0>[W] err[K]; //standard deviation of the linear equations

  //-------------------------------//
  //   unknown population          //
  //-------------------------------//

  vector[W] gamma;
  simplex[2] known_unknown[M];

  //-------------------------------//
  //   bias         //
  //-------------------------------//

  vector<lower=0> [num_batches]  bias_magnitude;
  vector[W] perturbation[num_batches];

================================================

Those parameter have these priors:

  //-------------------------------//
  //   topic probability           //
  //-------------------------------//

  for(m in 1:M) theta[m] ~ dirichlet(alpha);  // topic probability per document

  //-------------------------------//
  //   linear regression           //
  //-------------------------------//

  for(m in 1:M) for(k in 1:K) for(w in 1:W) if(counts[m,w]>0)
    counts_10[m,w] ~ lognormal(phi_hat_stable[m,k,w], err[k,w]); //prior on linear regression mean sigma

  for(k in 1:K) err[k] ~ cauchy(0, 2); //error on gene expression for sigma prediction

  //-------------------------------//
  //   unknown population          //
  //-------------------------------//

  for(m in 1:M) known_unknown[m] ~ dirichlet(k_n_hyper);

  //-------------------------------//
  //   cell isolation bias         //
  //-------------------------------//

  gamma ~ multi_normal(lg_mu, lg_sigma); // prior UN-known population

  for(b in 1: num_batches) perturbation[b] ~ gamma(bias_magnitude[b], 1/bias_magnitude[b]);

================================================

The whole model is attached.

Yes, extra parameters with no priors can severely mess up adaptation.
But they’re also just ill-defined and _shouldn’t_ fit.  Because HMC samples 
so efficiently it immediately identifies these “flat” parameters by running off 
to infinity, while other samplers slowly diffuse which can make it difficult to 
identify the problem.

the same scale as your posterior standard deviations.  normal(0, scale) would
work well.

could mess something up so it’s always best to remove them if you can.

> On Mar 23, 2016, at 8:24 PM, stefano <mangiol...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> I see. I will read the chapter, however from your answer I'm understanding that unbounded parameters (although with proper priors) are somehow harmful for the model.

> Is this correct?

The problem is improper posteriors, not unbounded parameters.
Too-thick or too-thin tails can also be a problem as can scales
well beyond unit scale (like normal(0, 1e-100) or normal(0, 1e100).
But something like y ~ normal(0, 1) has theoretically unbounded
support, but should sample just fine.

>
> To answer your question
>
> =================================================
>
> I have 7 parameters of which only one is part of the naive model (LDA with phi known), and thus necessary.
>
> //-------------------------------//
> // topic probability //
> //-------------------------------//
>
> simplex[K] theta[M]; // topic distribution for doc m
>
> //-------------------------------//
> // linear regression //
> //-------------------------------//
>
> vector<lower=1-0.1, upper=maxPoly+1+0.1>[M] sigma; //activation/disease state

We recomend against these kinds of interval-constrained priors.
Leave them unbounded and add a reasonable at least weakly
informative prior.

> vector<lower=0>[W] err[K]; //standard deviation of the linear equations
>
> //-------------------------------//
> // unknown population //
> //-------------------------------//
>
> vector[W] gamma;
> simplex[2] known_unknown[M];
>
> //-------------------------------//
> // bias //
> //-------------------------------//
>
> vector<lower=0> [num_batches] bias_magnitude;
> vector[W] perturbation[num_batches];
>
> ================================================
>
> Those parameter have these priors:
>
> //-------------------------------//
> // topic probability //
> //-------------------------------//
>
> for(m in 1:M) theta[m] ~ dirichlet(alpha); // topic probability per document
>
> //-------------------------------//
> // linear regression //
> //-------------------------------//
>
> for(m in 1:M) for(k in 1:K) for(w in 1:W) if(counts[m,w]>0)
> counts_10[m,w] ~ lognormal(phi_hat_stable[m,k,w], err[k,w]); //prior on linear regression mean sigma
>
> for(k in 1:K) err[k] ~ cauchy(0, 2); //error on gene expression for sigma prediction
>
> //-------------------------------//
> // unknown population //
> //-------------------------------//
>
> for(m in 1:M) known_unknown[m] ~ dirichlet(k_n_hyper);
>
Great variable name :-)

> //-------------------------------//
> // cell isolation bias //
> //-------------------------------//
>
> gamma ~ multi_normal(lg_mu, lg_sigma); // prior UN-known population
>
> for(b in 1: num_batches) perturbation[b] ~ gamma(bias_magnitude[b], 1/bias_magnitude[b]);
>
> ================================================
>
> The whole model is attached.

messages.subject: when do you need inits?
parts:
The other time that you might need inits is if the parameters are far from unit scale, for example if the posterior distribution is centered at 100 with a posterior sd of 1, or if the posterior distribution is centered at .01 with a posterior sd of .01. In these settings, default random inits can be so far from the meat of the posterior dist that Nuts can have trouble getting there.

(Another item for the manual, I guess…)

>
> Usually, you don't have to initialize unless there
> are modality problems or very tricky posteriors.
>
